title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed p. 19 (Night 230, continuing nights-229; the close of the night, with its closing formula, stood on printed pp. 20–21, which are missing from the only scan of volume 2, so the text breaks off mid-sentence), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 230 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Al-Amjad, having waited in vain for his brother until noon, weeps and laments, comes down from the mountain and goes into the city. There he learns that it is the City of the Magians, whose people worship fire, and that the City of Ebony lies a year away by land and six months by sea, where King Armānūs has married his daughter to a sultan named Qamar al-Zamān — al-Amjad's own father. Hearing his father named, he weeps and does not know where to turn; he hides to eat, can barely swallow for grief, and goes out to seek news of his brother. A Muslim tailor takes him in, consoles him and teaches him the trade. One day, washed and in clean clothes, he walks through the city and meets on his way a beautiful woman — and there the text breaks off: the rest of the night stood on pages missing from the only scan of this volume. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلثَّلٰثِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-thalāthīna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing-one of-the-thirty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and thirtieth night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula, in the edition's other way of naming a round number: al-mūfiya, the feminine active participle of awfā, Form IV of w-f-y, “to complete, make up”, is “the one completing”, and li- marks what it completes: the night that makes up the thirty after two hundred. The print spells thirty defectively, ثلثين, without the alif of thalāthīn, so it is pointed with a dagger alif. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْأَمْجَدَ لَمَّا مَكَثَ يَنْتَظِرُ أَخَاهُ الْأَسْعَدَ إِلَى نِصْفِ النَّهَارِ فَمَا عَادَ إِلَيْهِ فَخَفَقَ فُؤَادُهُ وَاشْتَدَّ بِهِ أَلَمُ الْفِرَاقِ وَأَفَاضَ دَمْعَهُ الْمُهْرَاقَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-Amjada lammā makatha yantaẓiru akhāhu al-Asʿada ilā niṣfi al-nahāri fa-mā ʿāda ilayhi fa-khafaqa fuʾāduhu wa-ishtadda bihi alamu al-firāqi wa-afāḍa damʿahu al-muhrāqa
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that al-Amjad, when he-stayed waiting-for his-brother al-Asʿad until (the) half (of) the-day, and-not he-returned to-him, then-throbbed his-heart, and-grew-hard on-him (the) pain (of) the-parting, and-he-made-overflow his-tears, the-poured-out.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when al-Amjad had waited for his brother al-Asʿad until midday and he had not come back to him, his heart began to pound, the pain of parting pressed hard upon him, and he let his tears pour freely.
sentences.n: The night opens by retelling where the last one stopped, almost word for word. lammā, “when”, with a past verb sets the scene, and its answer here opens with fa-, fa-khafaqa, “then his heart throbbed”: Classical Arabic leaves the answer of lammā bare, and the fa- is a habit of Middle Arabic narrative that will keep coming back. fa-mā ʿāda, “and he did not return”, is still part of the lammā clause: mā with a past verb is the plain negative of the past. makatha, “to stay”, with the imperfect yantaẓiru, “waiting”, says what he did while he stayed; niṣf al-nahār, “the half of the day”, is noon. ishtadda bihi, Form VIII of sh-d-d, “to grow severe upon him”: bi- marks the one it weighs on. al-muhrāq, “poured out”, is the passive participle of ahrāqa, an old by-form of arāqa, “to pour”. The sajʿ falls on al-firāq / al-muhrāq. The hamza of فؤاده and the shadda of واشتدّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَبَكَى وَنَادَى وَا أُخَيَّاهْ وَارَفِيقَاهْ وَاحَسْرَتَاهْ مَاكَانَ أَخْوَفَنِي مِنَ الْفِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-bakā wa-nādā wā ukhayyāh wā-rafīqāh wā-ḥasratāh mā kāna akhwafanī mina al-firāqi
sentences.l: And-he-wept and-called-out: O little-brother-ah! O companion-ah! O grief-ah! What was (it that) made-me-most-fearful of the-parting!
sentences.i: He wept and cried aloud, “Alas, my little brother! Alas, my companion! Alas, my sorrow! How I dreaded this parting!”
sentences.n: wā is the particle of nudba, the lament for the dead or the lost, and the name it laments takes the drawn-out ending -āh: -ā, the long cry, and a final h held in pause. ukhayy is the diminutive of akh, “brother”, the diminutive of tenderness, “dear little brother”; the print sets wā apart, وا اُخيّاه, and puts a damma on the alif and a shadda on the yāʾ of the second word; the hamza is ours. In وارفيقاه and واحسرتاه wā is joined to the word, as the print usually has it. rafīq is “companion, comrade on the road”, ḥasra “grief, bitter regret”. mā kāna akhwafanī is the exclamation of wonder, mā afʿala, “how … !”, with kāna slipped in to set it in the past: mā akhwafanī min, “how greatly I fear”, mā kāna akhwafanī, “how greatly I feared”; akhwafa is the afʿal of kh-w-f, “to fear”, and min marks what is feared. The print runs mā and kāna together as one word, ماكان, as it often does; that is kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَلَ مِنْ فَوْقِ الْجَبَلِ وَدَمْعُهُ سَائِلٌ عَلَى خَدَّيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma nazala min fawqi al-jabali wa-damʿuhu sāʾilun ʿalā khaddayhi
sentences.l: Then he-came-down from above the-mountain, and-his-tears (were) flowing on his-two-cheeks.
sentences.i: Then he came down from the mountain, his tears running down his cheeks.
sentences.n: wa-damʿuhu sāʾilun is a circumstantial clause, a ḥāl: wa- with a noun sentence describes the state he was in as he went, “while his tears were flowing”. min fawqi, “from on top of”: fawq, “above”, is a noun here, in the genitive after min. khaddayhi, “his two cheeks”, a dual; the -ni of the dual drops before the pronoun. The fatḥa on the jīm of الجبل, the ئ of سائل and the shadda of خدّيه are printed.

sentences.t: وَدَخَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مَاشِيًا فِيهَا حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى السُّوقِ
sentences.tr: wa-dakhala al-madīnata wa-lam yazal māshiyan fīhā ḥattā waṣala ilā al-sūqi
sentences.l: And-he-entered the-city, and-not he-ceased walking in-it until he-arrived at the-market.
sentences.i: He entered the city and walked on through it until he came to the market.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, from zāla, yazālu, with its predicate in the accusative, māshiyan, “walking”: “he kept on walking”. ḥattā with a past verb, “until”.

sentences.t: وَسَأَلَ النَّاسَ عَنِ اسْمِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَعَنْ أَهْلِهَا فَقَالُوا لَهُ هٰذِهِ تُسَمَّى مَدِينَةَ الْمَجُوسِ وَأَهْلُهَا يَعْبُدُونَ النَّارَ دُونَ الْمَلِكِ الْجَبَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-saʾala al-nāsa ʿani ismi al-madīnati wa-ʿan ahlihā fa-qālū lahu hādhihi tusammā madīnata al-Majūsi wa-ahluhā yaʿbudūna al-nāra dūna al-maliki al-jabbāri
sentences.l: And-he-asked the-people about (the) name (of) the-city and-about its-people; and-they-said to-him: This is-named (the) City (of) the-Magians, and-its-people worship the-fire instead-of the-King, the-Almighty.
sentences.i: He asked the people the name of the city and what its people were, and they told him, “This is called the City of the Magians, and its people worship fire instead of the Almighty King.”
sentences.n: saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿan marks what is asked about, and the person asked is a direct object, al-nāsa. ʿani ismi: ʿan takes a helping kasra before the joining alif of ism, which is not sounded. tusammā, passive of sammā, Form II of s-m-w, “to name”, keeps its second object in the accusative: tusammā madīnata al-Majūs, “it is named the City of the Magians”. The Majūs are properly the Zoroastrians; in the Nights the word means any fire-worshipper, and they are the villains of this part of the tale. dūna, “short of, instead of”. al-malik al-jabbār, “the King, the Compeller”, is God: al-Jabbār is one of His names. هذه is written without the alif after the hāʾ, and is pointed with a dagger alif. The hamza of وسأل and the shadda of الجبّار are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلَ عَنْ مَدِينَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ فَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّ الْمَسَافَةَ الَّتِي بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَهُ مِنَ الْبَرِّ سَنَةٌ وَمِنَ الْبَحْرِ سِتَّةُ أَشْهُرٍ
sentences.tr: thumma saʾala ʿan madīnati al-ābanūsi fa-qālū lahu inna al-masāfata allatī baynanā wa-baynahu mina al-barri sanatun wa-mina al-baḥri sittatu ashhurin
sentences.l: Then he-asked about (the) City (of) the-Ebony; and-they-said to-him: Indeed the-distance which (is) between-us and-between-it, by the-land (is) a-year, and-by the-sea six months.
sentences.i: Then he asked about the City of Ebony, and they told him, “The distance between us and it is a year by land and six months by sea.”
sentences.n: The City of Ebony is the home of the boys' father, Qamar al-Zamān, as the next sentence tells. inna, “indeed, truly”, opens the reported words after qāla, and its noun, al-masāfata, is accusative. bayna … wa-bayna, “between … and”, repeats bayna before each side. The city, madīna, is feminine, and Classical Arabic would say baynahā; the print has baynahu, “between it (m.)”, as if the speakers had al-ābanūs or the place in mind: loose agreement of this kind is common in Middle Arabic, and the very next clause goes back to the feminine, malikuhā, “its king”. min al-barr, “by land”, min al-baḥr, “by sea”: min here gives the way the distance is reckoned. sittatu ashhurin: from three to ten the counted noun is a genitive plural, and the numeral takes the feminine form with a masculine noun, shahr. The madda of الآبنوس, ābanūs, and the shadda of البرّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَمَلِكُهَا يُقَالُ لَهُ أَرْمَانُوسُ وَقَدْ صَاهَرَ الْيَوْمَ فِيهَا سُلْطَانًا وَجَعَلَهُ مَكَانَهُ وَذٰلِكَ الْمَلِكُ يُقَالُ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ وَهُوَ صَاحِبُ عَدْلٍ وَإِحْسَانٍ وَجُودٍ وَأَمَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-malikuhā yuqālu lahu Armānūsu wa-qad ṣāhara al-yawma fīhā sulṭānan wa-jaʿalahu makānahu wa-dhālika al-maliku yuqālu lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni wa-huwa ṣāḥibu ʿadlin wa-iḥsānin wa-jūdin wa-amānin
sentences.l: And-its-king, it-is-said to-him Armānūs; and-already he-has-become-related-by-marriage today in-it (to) a-sultan, and-made-him (in) his-place; and-that king, it-is-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān, and-he (is) possessor (of) justice and-beneficence and-generosity and-safety.
sentences.i: “Its king is called Armānūs. He has lately taken a sultan there for his son-in-law and set him in his own place, and that king is called Qamar al-Zamān, a man of justice and kindness, of generosity and security.”
sentences.n: yuqālu lahu, “it is said to him”, is the usual way of saying “he is called”: the passive of qāla with li- marking the one so called, and the name after it in the nominative. ṣāhara, Form III of ṣ-h-r, “to become related to someone by marriage”, takes that person as its object; ṣihr is a relation by marriage, and here the sultan has married the king's daughter. al-yawma, “today”, means “now, these days”. jaʿala … makānahu, “he made him (to stand in) his place”: makān is an accusative of place. ṣāḥib, “owner, companion”, before an abstract noun means “a man of”. The four nouns fall into two pairs, ʿadl wa-iḥsān / jūd wa-amān, and each pair ends on the rhyme -ān, closing the passage on a jingle; amān is the safety his subjects enjoy under him.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْأَمْجَدُ بِذِكْرِ أَبِيهِ بَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَصَارَ لَا يَعْلَمُ أَيْنَ يَتَوَجَّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-Amjadu bi-dhikri abīhi bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-ṣāra lā yaʿlamu ayna yatawajjahu
sentences.l: And-when heard al-Amjad of-(the)-mention (of) his-father, he-wept and-moaned and-complained, and-he-became not knowing where he-should-turn.
sentences.i: When al-Amjad heard his father spoken of, he wept, moaned and lamented, and he no longer knew where to turn.
sentences.n: samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”: with bi- the verb means hearing news of something rather than hearing a sound. abīhi, “his father”: akh and ab take a long vowel before a pronoun, here -ī in the genitive. anna, written وانّ with its shadda printed, is the verb “he moaned”, from ʾ-n-n, not the particle anna, “that”, as in the night before; it again pairs with bakā / ishtakā. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he came to be (not) knowing”, describes a state that sets in. yatawajjahu, Form V of w-j-h, “to turn one's face, head for”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اشْتَرَى مَعَهُ شَيْأً لِلْأَكْلِ وَدَخَلَ إِلَى مَوْضِعٍ يَتَوَارَى فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi ishtarā maʿahu shayʾan li-al-akli wa-dakhala ilā mawḍiʿin yatawārā fīhi
sentences.l: And-already he-had-bought with-him a-thing for-the-eating, and-he-went into a-place (where) he-could-hide in-it.
sentences.i: He had bought something to eat to take with him, and he went into a place where he could hide himself away.
sentences.n: wa-qad with a past verb, “and he had already”: the clause steps back to something done before. qad takes a helping kasra, qadi, before the joining alif of ishtarā, Form VIII of sh-r-y, “to buy”. maʿahu, “with him”, that is, to carry. shayʾan, “something”: the print writes شيأ, with the hamza on an alif, the edition's spelling of what is usually شيئا; it is kept. li-al-akl, “for eating”: li- of purpose. dakhala ilā, “to go into”: Classical dakhala takes its object directly, as in wa-dakhala al-madīnata earlier in this night, and the ilā is a looser usage. yatawārā, Form VI of w-r-y, “to hide oneself, be out of sight”: an unmarked relative clause after an indefinite noun, with fīhi, “in it”, pointing back to the place.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَعَدَ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَأْكُلَ فَتَذَكَّرَ أَخَاهُ فَبَكَى وَمَا أَكَلَ إِلَّا قَدْرَ سَدِّ الرَّمَقِ غَصْبًا
sentences.tr: thumma qaʿada wa-arāda an yaʾkula fa-tadhakkara akhāhu fa-bakā wa-mā akala illā qadra saddi al-ramaqi ghaṣban
sentences.l: Then he-sat-down and-wanted to eat, and-he-remembered his-brother and-wept, and-not he-ate except (the) amount (of) stopping-up the-last-breath, by-force.
sentences.i: Then he sat down and was about to eat, but he remembered his brother and wept, and he ate no more than he needed to keep himself alive, and that only by forcing himself.
sentences.n: an yaʾkula, “to eat”: an takes the subjunctive. mā … illā, “not … except”, means “only”. qadra saddi al-ramaq, “the amount of stopping up the ramaq”: ramaq is the last remnant of life, the breath left in the starving, and sadd al-ramaq, “stopping the gap of the last breath”, is the set phrase for eating just enough to stay alive. ghaṣban, “by force, against one's will”: ghaṣb is properly taking by force, and the accusative says how he ate, forcing it down. The shadda of الّا and of سدّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ يَمْشِي فِى الْمَدِينَةِ لِيَعْلَمَ خَبَرَ أَخِيهِ فَوَجَدَ رَجُلًا مُسْلِمًا خَيَّاطًا فِي دُكَّانٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma yamshī fī al-madīnati li-yaʿlama khabara akhīhi fa-wajada rajulan musliman khayyāṭan fī dukkānin
sentences.l: Then he-rose walking in the-city, so-that he-might-know (the) news (of) his-brother; and-he-found a-man, a-Muslim, a-tailor, in a-shop.
sentences.i: Then he got up and walked about the city to find out what had become of his brother, and he found a Muslim tailor in a shop.
sentences.n: qāma yamshī, “he rose (and went) walking”: qāma with an imperfect is “to set about”. li-yaʿlama, “so that he might know”: li- of purpose takes the subjunctive. rajulan musliman khayyāṭan, “a man, a Muslim, a tailor”: two descriptions stacked on rajul; in a city of fire-worshippers, a Muslim is a man he can trust. fī is spelled first with ى, فى, then with ي, as the print alternates. The shadda of خيّاطا is printed.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ عِنْدَهُ وَقَدْ حَكَى لِلْخَيَّاطِ قِصَّتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa ʿindahu wa-qad ḥakā li-al-khayyāṭi qiṣṣatahu
sentences.l: And-he-sat with-him, and-already he-told to-the-tailor his-story.
sentences.i: He sat down with him and told the tailor his story.
sentences.n: wa-qad ḥakā is best taken as “and he told”, the next step in the story, with qad loosely used: Middle Arabic narrative uses wa-qad with a past verb so, where Classical usage would want a past already completed. ḥakā li-, “to tell to”: li- marks the hearer. The shadda of قصّته is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَيَّاطُ إِنْ كَانَ وَقَعَ فِي يَدِ أَحَدٍ مِنَ الْمَجُوسِ فَمَا بَقِيتَ تَرَاهُ إِلَّا بِعُسْرٍ وَلَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يَجْمَعُ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khayyāṭu in kāna waqaʿa fī yadi aḥadin mina al-Majūsi fa-mā baqīta tarāhu illā bi-ʿusrin wa-laʿalla Allāha yajmaʿu baynaka wa-baynahu
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-tailor: If he-has fallen into (the) hand (of) one of the-Magians, then-not you-will-remain seeing-him except with-difficulty; and-perhaps God will-bring-together between-you and-between-him.
sentences.i: The tailor said to him, “If he has fallen into the hands of one of the Magians, you will see him again only with difficulty. But it may be that God will bring the two of you together.”
sentences.n: in kāna waqaʿa, “if he has fallen”: kāna with a second past verb sets the falling before the moment of speaking. waqaʿa fī yad, “to fall into the hand of”, to come into someone's power. fa-mā baqīta tarāhu: the answer of in opens with fa- because it begins with mā; baqiya, “to remain”, with an imperfect is “to go on (doing)”, and negated, “no longer”; baqīta, past in form, looks to the future here: “you will no longer”. illā bi-ʿusr, “except with difficulty”: bi- of manner. laʿalla, “perhaps”, takes its noun in the accusative, Allāha. jamaʿa bayna … wa-bayna, “to bring … together”. The shadda of ولعلّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ هَلْ لَكَ يَا أَخِي أَنْ تَنْزِلَ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu hal laka yā akhī an tanzila ʿindī
sentences.l: Then he-said to-him: Is (there) for-you, O my-brother, that you-lodge with-me?
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Would you like, my brother, to stay with me?”
sentences.n: hal laka an, “is there for you that”, is the polite form of asking “would you care to”: li- marks the one to whom the choice is offered. nazala ʿinda, “to come down at someone's”, is to lodge with him, as a traveller does.

sentences.t: قَالَ نَعَمْ فَفَرِحَ الْخَيَّاطُ بِذٰلِكَ وَأَقَامَ عِنْدَهُ أَيَّامًا وَهُوَ يُمَلِّيهِ وَيُصَبِّرُهُ وَيُعَلِّمُهُ الْخِيَاطَةَ حَتَّى صَارَ مَاهِرًا
sentences.tr: qāla naʿam fa-fariḥa al-khayyāṭu bi-dhālika wa-aqāma ʿindahu ayyāman wa-huwa yumallīhi wa-yuṣabbiruhu wa-yuʿallimuhu al-khiyāṭata ḥattā ṣāra māhiran
sentences.l: He-said: Yes. And-rejoiced the-tailor at-that; and-he-stayed with-him days, and-he (was) keeping-him-company(?) and-making-him-patient and-teaching-him the-tailoring, until he-became skilled.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, and the tailor was glad of it. So al-Amjad stayed with him for some days, while the tailor kept him company and consoled him and taught him the tailor's craft, until he became skilled at it.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to be glad of”: bi- marks the cause of the joy. aqāma ʿindahu: the one who stays is al-Amjad, and wa-huwa, “while he”, turns to the tailor; the pronouns shift without warning, as they often do in this prose. The first of the three verbs is uncertain. The print has يملّيه, with its shadda printed, and it is pointed here as yumallīhi, Form II of m-l-w: mallā is “to grant someone long enjoyment” of a thing or a companion, and so, perhaps, “to keep him company, cheer him”. The reading of the scan is itself not sure. The sense wanted beside yuṣabbiruhu, “he urged him to patience, comforted him” (Form II of ṣ-b-r), is surely “to divert, console”, which is yusallīhi, يسلّيه, with sīn for mīm; the print may have that slip, but the word is kept as it stands. yuʿallimuhu al-khiyāṭata, “he taught him tailoring”: ʿallama, Form II of ʿ-l-m, takes two objects, the pupil and the thing taught. ṣāra māhiran, “he became skilled”: ṣāra, “to become”, takes its predicate in the accusative. The shadda of ويعلّمه is printed.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ يَوْمًا إِلَى شَاطِئِ الْبَحْرِ وَغَسَلَ أَثْوَابَهُ وَدَخَلَ الْحَمَّامَ وَلَبِسَ ثِيَابًا نَظِيفَةً
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja yawman ilā shāṭiʾi al-baḥri wa-ghasala athwābahu wa-dakhala al-ḥammāma wa-labisa thiyāban naẓīfatan
sentences.l: And-he-went-out one-day to (the) shore (of) the-sea, and-washed his-garments, and-entered the-bath, and-put-on clothes clean.
sentences.i: One day he went out to the seashore and washed his clothes, then went into the bathhouse and put on clean clothes.
sentences.n: yawman, “one day”: an accusative of time. athwāb and thiyāb are both plurals of thawb, “garment”: the first is the plural of few, the second the common plural, and the storyteller uses one and then the other for variety. al-ḥammām is the public bathhouse. The ئ of شاطئ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ يَتَفَرَّجُ فِى الْمَدِينَةِ فَصَادَفَ فِي طَرِيقِهِ إِمْرَأَةً ذَاتَ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja mina al-ḥammāmi yatafarraju fī al-madīnati fa-ṣādafa fī ṭarīqihi imraʾatan dhāta ḥusnin wa-jamālin
sentences.l: Then he-went-out from the-bath, looking-about in the-city; and-he-chanced-upon in his-way a-woman, possessor (of) beauty and-loveliness […]
sentences.i: Then he came out of the bathhouse and strolled about the city to see the sights, and on his way he chanced upon a woman of beauty and loveliness […]
sentences.n: yatafarraju, Form V of f-r-j, “to look about for one's pleasure, to see the sights”: the imperfect after kharaja says what he went out doing. ṣādafa, Form III of ṣ-d-f, “to come upon by chance”, takes its object directly. imraʾa, “woman”, Classically begins with a joining alif that carries no hamza; the print writes it إمرأة, with a hamza under the alif and the middle hamza on an alif, the edition's spelling, and it is kept. dhāta ḥusnin wa-jamālin, “possessed of beauty and loveliness”: dhāt, the feminine of dhū, agrees with imraʾa in the accusative and governs the nouns after it in the genitive. A passage is skipped here for now. The rest of this night, with its closing formula, stood on pages 20 and 21 of this volume, which are missing from the only scan, so the text breaks off here, in the middle of the sentence.
